The Bible is the central sacred text of Christianity, comprising the Hebrew Bible, also called the Old Testament, and the New Testament. Written across more than a thousand years in Hebrew, Aramaic, and Greek, it contains law, prophecy, poetry, wisdom literature, and four Gospels narrating the life and teachings of Jesus. The Christian Bible is divided into two parts: the Old Testament, containing 39 books in the Protestant canon, and the New Testament, containing 27 books and focusing on Jesus and early Christian communities. The Hebrew Bible itself is organized into three sections: the Torah, or five books of law; the Prophets; and the Writings, covering creation, Israel's covenant history, poetry, wisdom, and messianic hope. The New Testament contains four Gospels—Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John—the Acts of the Apostles, Paul's letters to early churches, and other epistles culminating in Revelation. The Bible was written by many authors over centuries. Early Christians gradually recognized certain texts as divinely inspired, forming the canon, while rejecting others as apocryphal or heretical. Different Christian traditions recognize different canons: Protestants accept 66 books, Catholics and Orthodox Christians include additional apocryphal texts, creating canons of 73 or 81 books. Translations like the King James Version, Luther's German translation, and modern versions like the NIV and NRSV have shaped how readers encounter Biblical language and meaning across centuries.
